name: Coordinate the site day to day
summary: The superintendent runs each active site day by day: opening the site, planning the day against the lookahead, holding a start-up meeting with trade foremen, receiving deliveries, walking the work, sorting out conflicts and questions, booking labour, equipment and inspections, and writing the daily report. The assistant superintendent, field engineer and site administrator share the work. Weather, late or short-manned trades, missing information and changed conditions force constant re-planning, and a thin daily record weakens later delay and change claims.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian national general contractor of about 2,800 employees building institutional, commercial and industrial buildings, with about 220 active projects run from regional offices, a web-based project management platform and a construction ERP.
baseline.notes: Practice described for Ontario stipulated-price and construction-management projects on CCDC contract forms; Western and Atlantic projects follow the same pattern under their provincial lien and safety laws.

trigger: A working day starts on an active, mobilized site.
end_state: The site is secured, the signed daily report is filed and distributed, and any RFIs, change requests, labour, equipment and inspection requests raised that day have been passed on.

volume.seasonality: Highest from May to October, when sites work 10-hour days and some Saturdays; lower from December to February when some sites stop exterior work and holidays shut sites for about two weeks.

evidence.note: 220 active projects (organisation demand driver) x about 21 working days; low and high reflect 190 to 260 projects and the winter and summer swing.
Share of the role's time spent on daily site coordination, author's estimate; headcount from the organisation file. 120 superintendents x about 0.6.
Share of the role's time spent on daily site coordination, author's estimate; headcount from the organisation file. 90 assistant superintendents x about 0.45.
Share of the role's time spent on daily site coordination, author's estimate; headcount from the organisation file. 120 field engineers x about 0.33; the rest goes to RFIs, submittals and layout.
Share of the role's time spent on daily site coordination, author's estimate; headcount from the organisation file. 60 site administrators x 0.4.

systems.name: Project management platform (drawings, RFIs, submittals, daily logs, change events)
CPM scheduling software (Primavera P6, Microsoft Project)
BIM and clash detection tools (Revit, Navisworks)
Safety management system (hazard assessments, inspections, incidents, training records)
Equipment management (fleet register, rates, maintenance work orders)

resources.name: Pickup trucks for superintendents, foremen and safety staff
Site office trailers and sea containers
Telehandlers, skid steers and aerial work platforms

steps.name: Drive to site and open the trailer
steps.description: The superintendent drives the company pickup from home or the regional office to the site, unlocks the gate and the site office trailer, and checks overnight security, temporary heat or pumps before the trades arrive around 7:00.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Commute of 20 to 75 minutes to urban and suburban sites; superintendents are usually on site 30 to 60 minutes before the 7:00 start.

steps.name: Review the plan for the day
steps.description: In the trailer the superintendent opens the three-week lookahead, yesterday's daily report, the delivery and crane booking sheet and the inspection bookings, and lists which trades should be on site, in which areas, and what must happen today.

error.defect_description: A delivery or inspection booked by email is missed in the plan.

evidence.note: Practitioner knowledge of superintendent routines; Bird superintendent postings describe daily progress reporting and weekly subcontract meetings against the master schedule (postings not opened, so tier C).

steps.name: Check weather and decide whether work proceeds
steps.description: The superintendent checks the forecast and site conditions (rain, wind speed for crane lifts, temperature for concrete placing and curing) and decides whether planned pours, lifts and roofing go ahead or are cancelled and the trades re-sequenced.

error.defect_description: A pour or lift goes ahead in marginal weather and has to be stopped or repaired.

next.condition: heavy rain, high wind or extreme cold stops weather-sensitive work

evidence.note: About 8% of working days lose weather-sensitive work on Canadian building sites (rain, wind holds on cranes, cold-weather concreting limits); author's estimate, varies by region and season.

steps.name: Re-plan the day for weather
steps.description: The superintendent phones or texts trade foremen to cancel or move crews, reschedules the concrete supplier, pump and crane, moves crews to interior work where possible, and records the lost hours and the weather as a delay for later claims.

error.defect_description: A trade is not told and arrives to a cancelled pour.

next.condition: site rained out; only the record is made

evidence.note: Author's estimate of re-planning effort on a weather day; 40% of weather days assumed to stop most work on site.

steps.name: Sign in workers and orient new arrivals
steps.description: The site administrator checks the sign-in sheet or gate log against the expected trades, gives the site-specific orientation to new workers, checks their working-at-heights training card, and files the signed orientation forms.

error.defect_description: A new worker starts before orientation or with an expired training card.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA constructor duties and O. Reg. 297/13 working-at-heights training; company site orientation rule

evidence.note: Orientation of 2 to 5 new workers on a typical day at 10 minutes each plus sign-in check; author's estimate.

steps.name: Run the morning start-up meeting with trade foremen
steps.description: The superintendent gathers subcontractor and self-perform foremen at the trailer, walks through today's work areas, crane and hoist slots, deliveries, overlapping work and hazards, and agrees who works where so trades do not block each other.

error.defect_description: Two trades are given the same area or a hoist slot is double-booked.

control.basis: Constructor's duty under Ontario OHSA s.23 to coordinate trades; company pre-task coordination meeting

evidence.note: 15 to 30 minute morning huddles are the common practice on general contractor sites; author's estimate.

steps.name: Receive deliveries and book hoisting
steps.description: The assistant superintendent checks arriving trucks against the delivery schedule and purchase orders, directs them to the laydown area, books the telehandler, hoist or crane for offloading, signs the delivery tickets and notes shortages or damage.

error.defect_description: Short or damaged material is signed for as received.

evidence.note: Two to six deliveries a day on an active building site; telehandler offload time per delivery from author's estimate.

steps.name: Walk the work
steps.description: The superintendent walks every active area, compares progress with the lookahead, checks installed work for visible quality problems, housekeeping, guardrails and openings, and notes problems, trade manpower and photos on a tablet or notebook.

error.defect_description: A quality or safety problem in an area not walked is missed.

evidence.note: Most superintendents walk the site at least twice a day; time scales with building size; author's estimate.

steps.name: Check layout and installed work against drawings
steps.description: The field engineer checks gridlines, elevations, embeds and sleeves before pours, compares installed work with the current drawings, RFI answers and reviewed shop drawings, and photographs anything that does not match.

error.defect_description: A superseded drawing revision is used for the check.

evidence.note: Field engineer time on daily checks; author's estimate. FMI/PlanGrid found 5.5 hours a week per person spent looking for project data such as revised drawings (src cdive), which this step and the RFI process absorb.

steps.name: Decide what to do about issues found
steps.description: The superintendent reviews the notes from the walk and the field engineer's check and decides whether each issue can be fixed by a trade today, needs another trade to move, needs a question to the designer, is extra work, or is a safety incident.

error.defect_description: Extra work is treated as base scope and not recorded.

next.condition: trades conflict over space, sequence or damaged work
changed condition or owner-requested extra work
near miss, injury or property damage

evidence.note: Branch shares are the author's estimates. The RFI share is set so that site-raised questions are about half of the RFI process volume (0.14 x 4,600 project-days = about 640 site-raised questions a month before screening). FMI/PlanGrid report almost 5 hours a week per person managing disagreements (src cdive).

steps.name: Resolve a conflict between trades
steps.description: The superintendent meets the foremen involved at the work face, decides who goes first or who repairs damaged work, adjusts the sequence and hoist time, and confirms the decision by text or email so it is on record.

error.defect_description: A verbal decision is not recorded and later disputed in a back-charge.

next.condition: a trade is repeatedly short-manned or late

evidence.note: FMI/PlanGrid: almost 5 hours a week managing disagreements between stakeholders; time per conflict is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Write a notice to an under-performing trade
steps.description: The superintendent writes an email or site memo to the subcontractor's project manager stating the missed manpower or dates, the schedule impact and the required recovery, copies the project manager, and records it for the subcontractor performance file.

error.defect_description: Notice lacks dates and manpower facts needed later.

control.basis: Subcontract notice provisions (CCA 1 style): written notice before back-charge or default

evidence.note: Formal notices on about 3% of project-days (0.20 x 0.15); author's estimate.

steps.name: Raise a field question for an RFI
steps.description: The field engineer measures and photographs the conflict, writes a short description with grid references and a proposed solution, and passes it to the RFI process so it can be issued to the consultant.

error.defect_description: Question lacks references and is returned by the consultant.

evidence.note: Hand-off to the RFI workflow; author's estimate of drafting time at this point.

steps.name: Record a changed condition and notify the project manager
steps.description: The superintendent photographs the condition, records the time, crews and equipment affected, issues or requests a site instruction, and emails the project manager so a change notice can be raised within the contract notice period.

error.defect_description: Time and material records are incomplete and cost is not recovered.

control.basis: CCDC 2 Part 6 change provisions: prompt written notice of changes and claims

evidence.note: Author's estimate; changed conditions on about 1 in 9 project-days.

steps.name: Respond to an incident and notify safety
steps.description: The superintendent makes the area safe, arranges first aid, secures the scene if the injury is critical, phones the regional safety manager and starts the incident report so the safety team can investigate and report to regulators.

error.defect_description: Witness details or photos are not captured.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA s.51-52: notice of critical injury and accidents; scene preserved

evidence.note: Near misses, first aid and property damage events on about 3% of project-days; author's estimate.

steps.name: Book labour, equipment and inspections
steps.description: The assistant superintendent phones or emails the yard coordinator for equipment, sends the labour request for self-perform crews, books testing-agency and municipal inspections for tomorrow, and orders small materials.

error.defect_description: An inspection is booked for the wrong day or equipment is not ordered.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of daily booking work.

steps.name: Hold the weekly subcontractor coordination meeting
steps.description: Once a week the superintendent chairs a meeting with all trade foremen and project managers, reviews the three-week lookahead against the master schedule, open RFIs and submittals, safety items and manpower, and records actions in minutes.

error.defect_description: An action is not minuted and is forgotten.

evidence.note: One meeting a week, so 20% of project-days with a five-day week; duration is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Collect trade daily sheets and enter manpower
steps.description: The site administrator collects subcontractor foremen's daily sheets or texts, enters workers and hours by trade, equipment on site and visitors into the daily log in the project platform, and chases trades that did not report.

error.defect_description: Manpower is keyed wrongly or a trade is missing from the log.

evidence.note: Fieldwire describes trade foremen logging their own crews and the superintendent compiling the report; time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Write and sign the daily report
steps.description: At the end of the day the superintendent completes the daily report in the project platform: weather, manpower by trade, equipment, work done by area, deliveries, inspections, delays, visitors, incidents and photos, then signs it.

error.defect_description: Delays or extra work are left out of the report, weakening a later claim.

control.basis: Company project controls procedure: signed daily report every working day, kept as contract record

evidence.note: Content and end-of-day timing from Fieldwire; 45 minutes is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Walk the site and secure it for the night
steps.description: The assistant superintendent walks the perimeter, checks hoarding, fencing and gates, covers openings, checks temporary heat, pumps and fire extinguishers, makes sure the crane is weather-vaned, and locks the site and trailer.

error.defect_description: A gate or opening is left unsecured.

control.basis: O. Reg. 213/91 protection of the public and site security; company end-of-day checklist

evidence.note: Author's estimate of end-of-day checks.

steps.name: File the daily record and distribute it
steps.description: Next working morning the site administrator checks the daily report has been signed, files the timesheets and photos, and sends the report to the project manager; on Fridays the week's reports go to the scheduler and project accountant for the progress update.

error.defect_description: A report is filed unsigned or photos are missing.

next.condition: superintendent declares the building ready for deficiency review

evidence.note: Overnight wait to the office-hours administrator, longer after Fridays; 0.003 matches about 10 project completions a month out of 4,600 project-days.

exceptions.name: Weather stand-down
exceptions.description: Rain, wind or cold stops pours, lifts or roofing; the superintendent re-plans and in 40% of these days the site is rained out and only the record is made.

exceptions.name: Trade conflict escalated to a performance notice
exceptions.description: A repeatedly late or short-manned trade gets a written notice that feeds the subcontractor performance process.

exceptions.name: Site incident
exceptions.description: A near miss, injury or damage event takes the superintendent away from coordination for one to four hours.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from site opening to filed daily record
benchmarks.population: One project-day on a Canadian general contractor building site

evidence.note: The day's work fits in one 10 to 12 hour shift and the daily report is filed the next working morning; Friday reports wait over the weekend, which sets the p90. Fieldwire describes end-of-day completion of the report (src fieldwire).
FMI/PlanGrid Construction Disconnected survey; US population used as a proxy for Canada.

pain_points.description: Superintendents spend a large part of the day searching for current drawings and answers and resolving disagreements between trades, rather than planning ahead.

evidence.note: 5.5 hours a week looking for project data and almost 5 hours managing disagreements per person.

pain_points.description: Weather cancels pours and lifts at short notice and forces re-sequencing of crews, pumps and cranes.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of frequency; common experience on Canadian sites.

pain_points.description: The daily report is written at the end of a long day and often leaves out delays, extra work and manpower shortfalls that later matter for change orders and delay claims.

evidence.note: Fieldwire notes gaps or vague entries weaken a later delay claim.

pain_points.description: Manpower is re-keyed from trade daily sheets into the platform by the site administrator, and missing sheets have to be chased.

evidence.note: Common practice in 2019-2022 before trade foremen entered their own logs; author's estimate.

sources.title: Industry could be overspending $177B per year, study finds
sources.supports: FMI and PlanGrid 'Construction Disconnected' survey of 600 professionals (49% general contractors): 35% of time on non-optimal activities, more than 14 hours per person per week; 5.5 hours a week looking for project data, almost 5 hours managing disagreements, nearly 4 hours on mistakes needing rework; poor communication 26% and poor project information 22% of rework.

sources.title: Construction daily report forms: How field teams document daily work
sources.supports: Daily report is completed by the superintendent or foreman and finalised at the end of each workday; on larger projects each trade foreman logs their own crew and the superintendent compiles the site report; sections cover weather, crew and labour hours, subcontractors and visitors, equipment, materials, work performed, delays and safety incidents, photos and sign-off; daily reports are cited with schedules and correspondence as evidence in delay claims.

assumptions: The simulated median of about 1.3 days is above the 1.0-day benchmark because the simulator runs steps one after another; in practice the field engineer's checks, sign-in and the start-up meeting overlap the superintendent's walk (marked concurrent_with), so the real day is shorter.
A case is one project-day; every active project runs this process each working day, so step shares (weekly meeting on 20% of days, weather on 8%) are per-day probabilities.

The superintendent, assistant superintendent, field engineer and site administrator are the organisation file's roles; on small projects one superintendent covers two sites or an assistant superintendent acts as lead, so per-day hands-on time is an average across project sizes.

The staffing check uses 130 productive hours a month; site roles work about 190 hours a month in season (10-hour days and some Saturdays), so the stated FTE are lower than hands-on time x volume / 130 would suggest.
Subcontractor foremen take part in the start-up meeting and weekly meeting but are outside the organisation; their time is not counted.
Field level hazard assessments are done by each crew in hse-daily-hazard and are an input to the start-up meeting, not a step here.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (1.35 loading factor for salaried staff).
Practice described is Ontario; other provinces have equivalent constructor, orientation and incident-reporting rules.
